facts: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a possible House vote within days.

The resolution lists eight charges: three for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution, one for failing to minimize civilian casualties, one for overseeing 'extrajudicial killings' in strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, one tied to efforts to punish Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) over a video on refusing illegal orders, one for the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and one for illegally waging war against Yemen.
Hegseth called the articles a 'sham' and said, 'Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me.'
Trump told reporters, 'I'll stand by him... He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won.'
Impeachment and removal would require a House majority followed by a two-thirds vote (67 senators) in the Senate to convict.
Massie first tried to force a floor vote before the midterms, but Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) called an early recess, causing that resolution to expire; Massie reintroduced it afterward.
Hegseth campaigned for Ed Gallrein, who defeated Massie in the GOP primary.
Presumptive incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) has signaled support for the impeachment push.
ladder.analysis: The impeachment push centers on a decades-old, largely unresolved dispute over the War Powers Resolution, which requires presidential administrations to seek congressional authorization for military action but which presidents of both parties have routinely sidestepped. Massie's resolution attempts to use Hegseth's handling of strikes on Iran, Yemen, and alleged drug boats, along with the Maduro operation, as a test case for enforcing those limits. Because an outright Senate conviction requires 67 votes — a high bar even under divided government — the practical significance of the House vote is more symbolic and political than an imminent threat of removal, serving instead as a marker of how many Republicans are willing to break with the administration over war powers.

rep: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth calls the impeachment articles a 'sham,' saying efforts against Trump failed and 'it won't work with me.'

Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH) argues impeachment would be hypocritical since past administrations of both parties have ignored war powers limits, calling it 'scapegoating' Hegseth and favoring using the power of the purse instead.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), who filed the articles, argues Congress must hold the administration accountable for violating war powers and frames impeachment as simply 'firing someone.'

ladder.steelman: The split is less partisan than ideological: a Republican author (Massie) is leading the impeachment push against a Republican defense secretary over war-powers enforcement, while other Republicans defend Hegseth and some Democrats back removal — showing the fight is really about executive war authority, not a clean party-line battle.
ladder.implications: A House vote appears likely to proceed soon, and with Democratic support plus a handful of Republicans, passage in the House is plausible; however, conviction in the Senate remains a high bar requiring two-thirds support, making Hegseth's removal unlikely in the near term even if the House impeaches him.

facts: Stephen Miller, 41, began serving as White House chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles, 69.

Trump announced the change via Truth Social on Friday; administration officials had previously denied reports that Wiles was departing, and Trump had said last month there was "zero chance" he would replace her.

Miller previously served as deputy chief of staff and had been a longtime Trump aide, helping design first-term immigration policies including family separation at the border and the travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries.
Wiles was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff and had co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign; Trump had nicknamed her the "Ice Maiden."
The leadership change occurred days after Republicans suffered losses nationwide in the midterm elections.

Richard Walters, a deputy chief of staff and close Wiles ally, announced he is also leaving the administration; other recent departures include Harmeet Dhillon from the Justice Department and Katie Zacharia, who spent five days as press secretary.
In a 60 Minutes interview that aired over the weekend, Trump said of his mass deportation policy, "I think it was too tough... a lot of people think it's too tough."
Trump said he offered UFC president Dana White the White House press secretary job, then said he was "only kidding"; the two were scheduled to meet Monday.
ladder.analysis: Wiles, a pragmatic operator, had been credited by outside observers with moderating some of the administration's more disruptive impulses — working alongside former tech adviser David Sacks to let business leaders soften or beat back policies such as workplace immigration raids. Miller's ascension replaces that dynamic with someone whose career has centered on hardline immigration enforcement rather than deal-making with corporate interests, raising questions among lobbyists and executives about who will now have Trump's ear. The shift comes at a politically sensitive moment: it follows sweeping midterm losses for Republicans and a rare moment of public second-guessing from Trump himself about the toughness of his deportation agenda, creating a visible tension between the administration's midterm reckoning and its decision to elevate the policy's chief architect.
ladder.steelman: Coverage of the change suggests it is seen as more than a routine personnel shift, with business leaders uncertain about future access to Trump and observers noting the timing — coming just after Wiles's sudden exit and Republicans' heavy midterm losses.
ladder.implications: Expect close watching of whether corporate lobbyists find new channels of influence under Miller, whether immigration enforcement intensifies or is recalibrated given Trump's own midterm-era doubts, and whether further staffing turnover follows as the administration resets heading into the second half of the term.

ladder.analysis:
Nvidia sits at the center of the US-China AI competition: its chips power most advanced AI systems, and Washington has used export controls since 2022 to keep its top technology out of China on national-security grounds. Because of that strategic position, revelations about his personal relationship with a woman US officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset immediately raised questions that go beyond his private conduct — touching on whether sensitive information or policy access could have been exposed, and prompting both an internal corporate review and a federal investigation.

The story is still unfolding through multiple parallel tracks: an FBI inquiry, Nvidia's own investigation, a Singaporean probe into Megaspeed's chip-export practices, a shareholder lawsuit, and a congressional briefing request. None of these processes has yet produced public findings on what, if anything, was compromised, and Beijing has flatly denied the espionage characterization.
ladder.steelman: Regardless of how the personal and legal questions resolve, the episode highlights a structural risk inherent in concentrating critical AI supply chains and policy influence in a small number of executives with extensive cross-border business ties.
ladder.implications: Outcomes to watch include the FBI's findings on whether any security breach occurred, Nvidia's own investigation results, whether Huang appears before Congress next week, developments in the California shareholder lawsuit, and whether Singapore's probe into Megaspeed uncovers sanctions violations — any of which could affect Nvidia's stock, its relationship with Washington, and future US policy on chip exports to China.

stories.headline: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
body: Israel's 26th Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday, with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeking to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after neither bloc secured a majority in the October 27 election. Eisenkot, a former army chief, was tasked by President Isaac Herzog on Sunday with forming a government, having received more recommendations from Knesset members than Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension.

Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in the 120-seat parliament, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority. Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats between them — the United Arab List with eight and the Joint List with 11 — following a surge in Arab voter turnout. Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament. The outcome, widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, has created a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a new coalition is formed.

In his swearing-in speech, Netanyahu warned against a government that includes "supporters of terror and haters of Israel" and appealed for a national unity government to confront what he called the threat of "a nuclear Iran." Eisenkot sharply criticized Netanyahu's remarks as "delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful," saying he was "now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute." President Herzog urged lawmakers to "leave no stone unturned" and launch an investigation into the October 7 Hamas attacks, and called on party leaders to "make concessions" to avoid a repeat election.

High on the opposition's agenda is replacing the current Knesset speaker, Amir Ohana, a close Netanyahu ally, with Matan Kahana from Eisenkot's Yashar party. The opposition parties hold 67 seats, enough to install a consensus choice. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, is nominated to head the foreign affairs and defence committee, which will play a central role in drafting legislation on conscription of ultra-Orthodox men — a key election issue. More than 160 former top security officials warned that rightwing activists were planning to disrupt the swearing-in with violent attacks to prevent the speaker change.

Eisenkot has called for the formation of a "national emergency government" and proposed four principles for any party or MK to join his coalition: recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; acceptance of the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including currently exempt communities; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organisation with a commitment to dismantling its military and governing capabilities. These requirements present obstacles for potential partners. The ultra-Orthodox UTJ and Shas parties, which won 13 seats, fiercely oppose changes to military conscription exemptions. The Arab parties, which emphasize equal rights for Israel's Arab citizens and do not recognize Hamas as a terrorist organisation, have offered support — the United Arab List willing to join a coalition, the Joint List offering parliamentary backing from outside — but Lieberman has refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.

If neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu forms a coalition, another round of elections could follow. Eisenkot has acknowledged that some election promises will have to be broken, saying, "No one will be able to fulfil all the [campaign] promises they made, and all of us will need to compromise." Protests have urged Jewish-Israeli opposition parties to prioritize unseating Netanyahu over excluding Palestinian-led parties from government.

stories.headline: October CPI rises more than expected, complicating Fed's inflation fight
body: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, exceeding economists' expectations and delivering fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday that the consumer price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, above the 0.3% forecast by economists surveyed by Dow Jones. Stripping out volatile food and energy, core CPI rose 0.3%, also topping the 0.2% estimate. The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%.

The Bureau did not estimate a yearly rate because the government shutdown last year prevented it from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, leaving no comparable figure. Bank of America, using an assumed baseline, estimated annual growth rates of 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core, both 0.1 percentage point higher than September and well above the Fed's 2% target. Among components, the energy index rose 0.7% (gasoline up 1%, natural gas down 0.8%), food accelerated 0.5%, transportation services jumped 0.8%, and shelter costs rose 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the headline increase. Used cars and trucks fell 1.2%, while new vehicle prices increased 0.2%.

The report comes at a critical juncture for the Fed. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was 'around 0.3.' Hours later, that's exactly what happened. Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking after the report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases and called the CPI 'higher than expected.' She added, 'It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall.' Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who does not vote on rates this year, said inflation is defying expectations and that the AI data center build-out 'is, to my eyes, starting to look more just like old-fashioned demand overheating.' He did not commit to a rate stance but said current conditions could warrant action.

Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes, said: 'This was the report the market could least afford to see. A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer.' The Fed voted 10-2 in October to hold its benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data. Economic growth remains strong, with third-quarter GDP at 3.4% and the Atlanta Fed tracking 3.5% for the fourth quarter. Nonfarm payrolls expanded by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate edged lower to 4.1%.

Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau said the report would 'effectively lock in another 25bp hike' in December, absent an indisputably soft 0.1% monthly print. A net 37% of businesses responding to the October National Federation of Independent Business survey reported plans to raise prices in the next three months, the highest level since July 2022. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is due later in November, and Logan said she is worried it could also move higher.

stories.headline: Fed's Waller signals December rate hike, opens door to half-point increase; Logan calls for two quarter-point moves
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Tuesday he is leaning toward a rate increase in December and would support a larger-than-usual half-percentage-point hike if inflation readings come in higher than forecast, warning that failing to follow through on expected tightening would risk the central bank's credibility. Speaking in London, Waller noted that the October consumer price index, released earlier Tuesday, showed headline inflation of 0.4% and core inflation of 0.3%—both 0.1 percentage point above the Dow Jones consensus. "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," Waller said, adding that a 50-basis-point hike "should be considered at the December meeting" if data come in stronger.

Waller emphasized that the precise timing of rate increases matters less than ensuring promised hikes are eventually carried out. "When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings," he said. "If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way." He characterized the economy as growing at a healthy pace with a solid labor market. Traders after the CPI report fully priced in a quarter-point hike in December and assigned 12.5% odds of a half-point move.

Separately, Dallas Federal Reserve President Lorie Logan said the central bank needs to deliver at least two more quarter-percentage-point rate increases to bring down inflation, and may need to move more rapidly this winter. "It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases," Logan said in remarks prepared for an energy conference. She noted that October core consumer prices rose 0.3%, a pace that if sustained would translate to year-over-year inflation above 4%, well above the Fed's 2% target. "Excess inflation is unacceptable," she said, adding that "tighter policy will be necessary to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for inflation and employment."

Logan supported the Fed's decision to skip a rate hike in October, saying gradual increases allow households, businesses, and markets to adapt and reduce the risk of slowing the economy more than necessary. However, she warned that the longer above-target inflation persists, the greater the risk it becomes baked into behavior. "The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment," she said. "It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall." The Fed's next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9.

The remarks from Waller and Logan come after the Federal Open Market Committee held rates steady at its October meeting, a decision that was not unanimous—Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented. Multiple Fed officials have recently counseled patience while stressing the need to bring inflation back to target. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday the Fed must be careful not to let the economy run too hot.

stories.headline: Stocks fall and Treasury yield reclaims 5% after hot CPI data fuels rate-hike bets
body: Stocks fell broadly on Tuesday after October inflation data came in hotter than expected and a key Federal Reserve official opened the door to a possible half-point rate increase next month. The S&P 500 traded down 0.9%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 302 points, or 0.6%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.6%. Nvidia, which slid 6%, dragged down all three major averages after CEO Jensen Huang admitted over the weekend to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The retreat came one day after the S&P 500 posted its best day since April.

The consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% gain economists polled by Dow Jones had expected. Core CPI — which excludes volatile food and energy costs — increased 0.3%, compared with expectations for a 0.2% advance. Annual figures were not provided for Tuesday's report because of the 2025 government shutdown. The stronger-than-expected CPI print renewed inflation fears and sent the 10-year Treasury note yield back above 5% as traders worried that interest rate increases could become more likely in 2027.

Earlier Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in a speech in London that he thinks a December rate hike is likely and opened the door to a possible half-point increase amid persistent inflationary pressures. "While the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does," he said. Traders now see a December rate hike as a near certainty and also expect at least a quarter-point hike at some point next year.

"The CPI print said perhaps inflation is going to be a little stickier for a little longer," said Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management. "There's an extrapolation that maybe the Fed's going to have to hike rates more aggressively next year." Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer at Regan Capital, said the strong jobs report for October gave the Fed cover to keep raising rates without harming the labor market. "The big driver of inflation has been oil prices, and we don't think the Iran conflict will end anytime soon, which means that oil prices and inflation are likely to stay elevated for the foreseeable future," he added.

The push and pull in markets comes after a rocky week in which traders grew concerned about a potential slowdown in data center buildouts after Democrats posted big victories in the midterm elections. While oil prices and bond yields fell after the midterms on hopes the Iran conflict would end sooner, Weinand said he does not expect the Trump administration to quickly resolve the conflict. "Stocks have taken a beating of late and have seen a large rotation out of AI plays and into more durable and defensive sectors like healthcare," he said. "This has roiled some leveraged funds and momentum players, but earnings should continue to benefit from high levels of government and corporate spending."

stories.headline: Anthropic sets IPO range valuing AI company at up to $1.3 trillion
body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has set the stage for an initial public offering that could value the firm at between $1.1 trillion and $1.3 trillion. The company plans to offer shares at $70 to $78 each on New York's Nasdaq exchange, aiming to raise up to $64 billion.

The valuation range, while enormous, falls short of the roughly $2 trillion that some backers had predicted earlier this year, as reported by the Financial Times. At the top end, Anthropic would be valued at about $1.3 trillion, below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket and AI company, which listed its shares in June at nearly $1.8 trillion.

Anthropic is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's U.S. midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns that a Democrat-led Congress could slow the development of AI and the buildout of data centers. Broader fears persist over whether the billions of dollars being poured into AI will ultimately pay off.

In its most recent financial results for the six months ending June 30, Anthropic reported a surge in revenue to $16.2 billion, up from $1.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. However, its pre-tax loss ballooned to $80.7 billion from $12.9 billion.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, described the $64 billion target as 'fairly bullish' given 'the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week.' She told Reuters: 'It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there.'

Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others, all of whom previously worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

stories.headline: NFL trade deadline: Jaguars acquire Jordan Davis; Vikings explore QB market; Bengals deal falls through
body: The Jacksonville Jaguars made a series of defensive acquisitions Monday, headlining the day with a blockbuster trade for Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis. According to multiple reports, the Jaguars sent multiple draft picks, including a first-round pick in the 2027 draft, to the Eagles for Davis. The Jaguars also added Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III from the Atlanta Falcons in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, and acquired defensive tackle Davon Godchaux from the New Orleans Saints for a 2028 sixth-round pick. The moves come as Jacksonville sits at 6-2 and positions itself as a Super Bowl contender.

The Minnesota Vikings, coming off a Monday night loss to the Buffalo Bills in which quarterback Carson Wentz struggled, are actively exploring the quarterback trade market. According to Yahoo Sports, the Vikings have inquired with the Las Vegas Raiders about a reunion with Kirk Cousins, who played for Minnesota from 2018 to 2023 and made three Pro Bowls. Cousins has thrown for 2,340 yards, 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions in nine games this season for the 4-5 Raiders. The Vikings have also shown interest in Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones, who has 1,722 passing yards, six touchdowns and 10 interceptions in nine games. Jones played for Minnesota in 2024 after being released by the New York Giants.

A reported trade between the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles for edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie fell through. The deal, which would have sent Ebiketie to Cincinnati for a 2027 sixth-round draft pick, was initially reported but later fell apart. Bengals head coach Zac Taylor said Monday, "Nothing. We're good," when asked about the team's plans at the trade deadline. Ebiketie, 27, signed a one-year deal with the Eagles in March and has 23 total tackles and three tackles for loss in nine games this season.

Other trades included the Detroit Lions acquiring safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets for a 2028 sixth-round pick, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter. Cisco, 26, has 23 tackles, a pass defended and a forced fumble in nine games this season. The Jaguars also confirmed that wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. is not being traded, per ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, despite speculation. Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones told 105.3 The Fan that the team does not expect to make a "significant" trade.

Several notable injuries were reported Monday. Los Angeles Rams All-Pro receiver Puka Nacua is expected to be placed on injured reserve with MCL and PCL sprains in his right knee and turf toe, head coach Sean McVay announced. Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs will undergo surgery for a fractured finger and is expected to miss up to three weeks, per CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz. Arizona Cardinals quarterback Gardner Minshew is feared to have a torn UCL in his throwing arm and could be out for the season, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. The Cardinals signed quarterback Josh Johnson off the Cleveland Browns' practice squad and will turn to rookie Carson Beck as starter. Cardinals wide receiver Michael Wilson will miss the rest of the season with a neck injury, head coach Mike LaFleur said. Baltimore Ravens head coach Jesse Minter said Jacoby Brissett is expected to start in Week 10 after the team acquired him from the Cardinals last week.

Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, who has 656 rushing yards and eight touchdowns this season, remains a potential trade target. The New England Patriots have been suggested as a logical suitor, especially after Rhamondre Stevenson's knee injury. Taylor thanked fans after Sunday's loss, saying, "This place helped shape me into the man I am today." The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

stories.headline: Wenger considers running against Infantino for FIFA presidency
body: Former Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger is considering standing against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, according to sources close to the Frenchman. Wenger, 77, currently serves as FIFA's head of global development and has been urged by senior figures in European football to run. The deadline for candidates to confirm their candidacy for the election, scheduled for March, is 18 November.

Wenger's potential candidacy comes amid a crisis for Infantino, triggered by the backlash against his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors. The proposal, known as the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), was withdrawn after widespread opposition. Wenger distanced himself from the plan, stating, 'I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports. The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent FIFA that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity.'

Infantino retains support in South America, Africa, and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the 'vast, vast majority' of world football. He received a major re-election boost when all 54 African member associations backed him after he promised an increase in funding. However, Wenger has a global profile, including in Africa, where he is known as a champion of African players during his time at Arsenal. His support for an expanded 48-team World Cup to drive development beyond traditional powers has been well received on the continent.

If Wenger stands, he would have the backing of UEFA, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino. Some of his supporters have told BBC Sport that they would be happy for him to win the election and then stand down before serving a full four-year term. Sources close to Wenger say he is yet to decide whether to stand, and they still believe Infantino is favourite to win a fourth and final term.

Other candidates have already entered the race. Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first to put his name forward in October. Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand. Meanwhile, FIFA has said that 'key documents' relating to the World Cup stake sale plan will be made available to members of its council, but they must travel to its Zurich base and access will be under 'strict protocols'. UEFA gave FIFA until 2 November to release details about the FFE proposal and answer questions about its decision-making, following a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned plot but failed to explain how it was devised.

stories.headline: Bengals trade with Eagles fails hours before deadline
body: The Cincinnati Bengals' proposed trade to acquire Philadelphia Eagles outside linebacker Arnold Ebiketie fell through hours before Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz. The Bengals had agreed to send a 2027 sixth-round pick to the Eagles for the 27-year-old defender, but the deal collapsed for reasons unrelated to a physical or performance issue.

Ebiketie signed a one-year, $7.3 million contract with Philadelphia in March after spending his first four seasons with the Atlanta Falcons. In nine appearances this season, he recorded 25 tackles and two quarterback hits, and he has 16.5 career sacks. The trade would have added another pass rusher to Cincinnati's defensive rotation as the team looked to strengthen its linebacker corps.

The failed transaction carries significant implications for the Bengals' draft plans. Because Philadelphia originally signed Ebiketie as a compensatory free agent, acquiring him would have counted against Cincinnati's compensatory pick formula. The Bengals lost three qualifying compensatory free agents this offseason—Trey Hendrickson, Joseph Ossai and Noah Fant—while signing two qualifying players, Bryan Cook and Boye Mafe. Cordell Volson does not qualify.

Avoiding the deal preserves Cincinnati's projected third-round compensatory selection tied to Hendrickson's $28 million annual contract with the Baltimore Ravens. The Bengals entered the deadline exploring multiple options to bolster their defense but ultimately will not add Ebiketie to their roster.

stories.headline: Cooper Flagg scores 43, makes NBA history in Mavericks win
body: Dallas Mavericks second-year star Cooper Flagg delivered a historic performance Monday night, scoring a season-high 43 points along with 10 rebounds, six assists, three steals and three 3-pointers to lead Dallas to a 125-122 victory over the Indiana Pacers.

Flagg, who turns 20 next month, became only the second teenager in NBA history to record at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a single game, according to the NBA's official X account. The only other player to reach those milestones as a teenager was future Hall of Famer Kevin Durant, who posted 42 points, 13 rebounds and six assists in the final game of his rookie season with the Seattle SuperSonics in 2007-08.

Selected first overall in the 2025 NBA draft out of Duke, Flagg was named NBA Rookie of the Year last season after averaging 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists per game. In his sophomore campaign, he has elevated his play, averaging 25.9 points, 6.9 rebounds, 6.9 assists and 2.2 steals per contest through the first 10 games.

Monday's performance also marked the 14th game of Flagg's career in which he scored at least 30 points, putting him second all-time among players who have recorded 30-point games before turning 20. The only player ahead of him is LeBron James, who accomplished the feat 20 times as a teenager. With his 20th birthday still a month away, Flagg has time to add to that total.

The Mavericks, who missed the playoffs each of the previous two seasons and won only 26 games during Flagg's rookie campaign, currently sit ninth in the Western Conference with a 7-4 record, placing them firmly in playoff contention.

stories.headline: FDA approves Bayer's asundexian, first factor XIa inhibitor, for stroke prevention
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved Bayer's asundexian, a once-daily oral pill to be sold under the brand name Sunharbo, for reducing the risk of recurrent stroke in certain adults. The drug is the first approved in the novel class of factor XIa inhibitors, which are designed to prevent blood clots without increasing the risk of major bleeding, a limitation of many existing blood thinners.

The FDA cleared Sunharbo for use in combination with antiplatelet therapy in adults who have had a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke—a stroke caused by a clot that did not originate in the heart—or a high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA). The approval is based on the phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE trial, which enrolled 12,327 adults. Over a median treatment period of 14.2 months, 6.2% of patients receiving Sunharbo experienced a recurrent ischemic stroke, compared with 8.4% of those on placebo, representing a 26% relative risk reduction. The rate of major bleeding was similar between groups: 1.9% for Sunharbo versus 1.7% for placebo. Diarrhea was the most common adverse reaction, occurring in at least 3% of patients. The FDA does not recommend Sunharbo with combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inducers, such as carbamazepine, or in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment, and advises withholding the drug at least 24 hours before elective surgery or invasive procedures.

The approval marks a significant advance in stroke prevention, a field that has seen little innovation in the past two decades. Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death and a leading cause of disability in the United States, with about 795,000 Americans experiencing a stroke each year. Roughly 1 in 10 ischemic stroke survivors will have another stroke within a year, and 1 in 5 within five years. "Stroke remains a very significant health burden in the United States, and the need for continued innovation is abundantly clear," said Sebastian Guth, chief operating officer of Bayer Pharmaceuticals and president of Bayer U.S. Hylton V. Joffe, director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, said in a statement: "Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in the United States, and survivors are at risk of having another stroke."

Asundexian works by inhibiting factor XIa, a protein involved in the coagulation cascade, with the goal of preventing the formation of harmful clots while interfering as little as possible with the body's natural repair mechanisms. Christoph Koenen, M.D., Bayer's chief medical officer, explained that genetic evidence—showing that people with naturally lower levels of factor XI have fewer cardiovascular events—supported the target. The drug had previously received its first worldwide approval in China in late October. Bayer's approval comes as the company faces generic competition to its established anticoagulant Xarelto and its eye treatment Eylea. A rival factor XIa inhibitor, milvexian, being developed by Bristol Myers Squibb and Johnson & Johnson, is in phase 3 trials for secondary stroke prevention. Bayer said it is ready for a U.S. launch at scale, with an established commercial and medical team. A 30-day supply of Sunharbo is listed at $748.50.

stories.headline: Anthropic sets IPO price range, launches Claude Meetings office suite
body: Anthropic on Tuesday set an initial public offering price range of $70 to $78 per share for 825 million Class A shares, implying a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.404 trillion. The offering is expected to raise between $57.75 billion and $64.35 billion, with net proceeds estimated to reach $84.6 billion to $93.7 billion if underwriters exercise an option to buy additional shares. The company plans to begin trading on the Nasdaq near November 19 under the ticker symbol “ANT,” with up to 20% of shares allocated to retail investors. The IPO comes despite volatile markets and a broader pullback from AI investing, and investors will watch Anthropic’s valuation as a gauge of the AI boom’s strength.

In a separate private sale, Anthropic agreed to sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC, with Google and Nvidia each investing $10 billion. The updated filing also revealed that co-founders CEO Dario Amodei, president Daniela Amodei, chief compute officer Tom Brown, Anthropic Institute head Jack Clark, chief science officer Jared Kaplan, chief architect Sam McCandlish, and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah are each selling nearly 3.4 million shares, which at the $74 midpoint of the price range would net roughly $250 million each. As a public benefit corporation, founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% voting power, and the Long-Term Benefit Trust will elect a board majority, limiting influence for Class A buyers.

The company reported run-rate revenue of $81 billion by the end of October, up about $10 billion from the end of September. Third-quarter revenue was $17 billion, and nine-month revenue reached $33.2 billion. Anthropic posted a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, with compute and infrastructure commitments of $900.9 billion, and holds nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments. The updated filing also adopted language from a Trump administration executive order, using “super intelligence” and “SI” interchangeably with “artificial intelligence” and “AI.” OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after raising $11 billion.

Alongside the IPO news, Anthropic unveiled a new AI-powered office suite at a San Francisco event on Tuesday, targeting non-technical knowledge workers. The suite includes Claude Meetings, which joins video calls as a visible participant to draft plans, map timelines, answer questions, and access connected apps in real time, then provides meeting notes and action items afterward. Claude Whiteboards offers a collaborative real-time board where teams can brainstorm with Claude and turn results into documents or slide decks, and Claude Sheets lets teams create and edit spreadsheets with Claude handling setup and direct cell edits. Claude Meetings is available in beta on Team and Enterprise plans, initially supporting Google Meet, while Whiteboards and Sheets are in beta on all paid plans across web, desktop, and mobile. The company also made Claude Data (formerly Claude Dashboards) generally available to all paid plans, enabling users to query data and receive dashboards, written stories, or narrated videos.

Anthropic introduced interactive connectors that allow users to open full versions of apps from partners such as Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude, embedding existing workflows into the same workspace. The company’s Model Context Protocol marketplace now includes more than 9,000 plugin options. Nicholas Lin, an Anthropic product lead, said Claude Code “changed how engineers work a year ago” and that the company now aims to close the adoption gap for non-developers, noting “there’s still a lot of friction when it comes to adopting AI for non-developers.” The tools follow similar moves by Google, OpenAI, and Meta as AI companies compete to build office suites that challenge Microsoft and Google. Anthropic faces pressure to generate revenue and drive engagement ahead of its IPO, and these products represent some of its first native offerings for non-technical workers.
